title: Sustaining South Africa’s Progress in the Next Phase of the HIV Fight
gist: CSIS commentary on South Africa's June 2026 lenacapavir PrEP rollout: early uptake is strong (about 79,000 started, 98% choosing the injection) and could bring epidemic control by 2039, but US funding cuts, exclusion from the Gilead-Global Fund access deal and uncertain local generic manufacturing threaten sustainability.

insights.claim: South Africa began offering twice-yearly lenacapavir PrEP in June 2026 to about 450,000 patients at 360 government clinics with Global Fund and Children's Investment Fund Foundation support; by October 15 just under 79,000 people had started and about 98 percent of new clients chose the injection over the daily pill.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Strong preference for long-acting PrEP signals large latent demand for injectable prevention.

insights.claim: Researchers estimate South Africa must initiate and sustain 1-2 million people per year on lenacapavir for five years, which could bring HIV incidence below the 0.1 percent elimination threshold by 2039, versus about 30 years on the current path.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defines the volume of doses needed, a demand marker for Gilead and generic licensees.

insights.claim: Gauteng exhausted its initial lenacapavir allocation and was replenished, with nearly 35,000 people on it by October 4 and stock projected for more than 114,000 by March 2027.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Supply, not demand, is the near-term constraint.

insights.claim: Until early 2025 about 17 percent of South Africa's HIV services and nearly 60 percent of its PrEP efforts were backed by US PEPFAR/USAID funding; most PEPFAR funding ended September 30, 2026, with all to cease by end of March 2027, and the DREAMS partnership has been terminated.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Funding gap shifts burden to the South African government and the Global Fund.

insights.claim: The US joined the Global Fund and Gilead in a partnership to provide long-acting PrEP to up to 3 million people across sub-Saharan Africa, but South Africa was excluded from the country list.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: South Africa's access depends on Global Fund doses and its own procurement.

insights.claim: Lenacapavir costs South Africa roughly $60 per person per year with Global Fund support, while a locally made generic could cost $40 or less; some local producers are declining to seek a Gilead licence because the long-term market may not justify new injectable manufacturing capacity.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Injectable capex risk may push procurement to the six existing Gilead licensees; generics expected in 2027.

insights.claim: South Africa's experience will be a test case for how countries scale long-acting PrEP as the US shifts toward bilateral compacts under the America First Global Health Strategy.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Outcome informs global health procurement models and demand forecasts for long-acting HIV prevention.
